title: Design Skiplist
statement:
Build a class `Skiplist` that stores a multiset of integers (the same value may be stored several times) as a skip list: a stack of sorted linked lists in which each higher list keeps a random subset of the nodes of the list below it, so a search can skip ahead quickly. Do not rely on any library ordered set, map or tree.

- `Skiplist()` creates an empty structure.
- `search(target)` returns `true` when at least one copy of `target` is stored, and `false` otherwise.
- `add(num)` stores one more copy of `num`.
- `erase(num)` removes a single copy of `num` and returns `true`. When no copy of `num` is stored, it changes nothing and returns `false`.

Each operation should take O(log n) expected time, where n is the number of stored values.
constraints: At most 5 * 10^4 calls in total are made to search, add and erase
notes:
## Intuition

A single sorted linked list makes every operation walk up to n nodes. A skip list stacks extra "express" lists on top: when a node is added it flips coins and joins level 1, then level 2 with chance 1/2, level 3 with chance 1/4, and so on. A search starts on the highest level, runs right while the next value is still too small, then drops a level. Each level roughly halves the remaining distance, so the expected walk is O(log n). (Keeping a plain list of values and scanning it is the simple, slow alternative.)

## Approach

1. Keep a `head` sentinel with `maxLevel` forward pointers and the current number of used levels, `level`.
2. `predecessors(target)`: from the top level down, move `node` forward while the next value is less than `target`, and record the last node visited on each level in `update`.
3. `search(target)`: the node right after `update[0]` on the bottom level is the first value at least `target`; check whether it equals `target`.
4. `add(num)`: pick a random `height` by coin flips, raise `level` if needed, and splice the new node in after `update[i]` on each of its levels.
5. `erase(num)`: if the first node not below `num` does not hold `num`, return `false`. Otherwise unlink it from every level it is on, drop empty top levels, and return `true`.

## Example 1, step by step

After `add(1)`, `add(2)`, `add(3)` the bottom list is `1 → 2 → 3` (higher levels depend on the coin flips but never change the answers). `search(0)`: every value is at least 0, so `update[0]` is `head` and the candidate is `1`, not `0`: `false`. `add(4)` appends 4. `search(1)` finds candidate `1`: `true`. `erase(0)` sees candidate `1`, so nothing is removed: `false`. `erase(1)` unlinks the node holding 1 on each of its levels: `true`. `search(1)` now finds candidate `2`: `false`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(log n) expected per operation: each level skips about half of the nodes below it.
- Space: O(n) expected: a node has 2 pointers on average.

## Pitfalls

- Duplicates must be kept, so `add` never rejects an existing value, and `erase` removes only one node.
- Move forward with `<`, not `<=`: the node after `update[i]` must be the first one not below the target, or `search` and `erase` would already be past it.
- When the new node is taller than `level`, its upper predecessors are `head`; filling `update` with `head` covers that.
- Cap the coin flips at `maxLevel` so the pointer arrays never overflow.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `head` | sentinel node whose `next[i]` starts level `i` |
| `maxLevel` | most levels a node may have (16 is plenty for 5 * 10^4 values) |
| `level` | number of levels currently in use |
| `update` | for each level, the last node whose value is below the target |
| `node` | the walker in `predecessors`, or the node being added or removed |
| `candidate` | first bottom-level node not below `target` |
| `height` | number of levels the new node joins |
